articles.title: Translating base editors: a decade of progress from the bench to the clinic.
articles.abstract: A decade has passed since the initial description of cytosine base editors in 2016. This new class of gene editors, utilizing DNA damage intermediates beyond double-stranded DNA breaks, fundamentally shifted the paradigm of gene editing from stochastic disruption to precise chemical correction. Since then, the field has rapidly matured, with the development of optimized base editors with improved editing efficiency, targeting scope, precision and specificity, as well as the subsequent generation of adenine base editors and prime editors. Base editors have not only become widely used research tools but have served as foundational platforms for biotechnology companies developing human therapies. Today, base editors are being deployed in trials for a diverse list of indications including sickle cell disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, inborn errors of metabolism, leukaemias and cardiovascular indications. This Review critically examines the 'bench-to-bedside' trajectory of base editors, detailing their mechanistic evolution and expanding role in treating human disease.

articles.title: Engineering monocytes and macrophages for therapeutic control.
articles.abstract: Engineered monocytes and macrophages are emerging as therapeutic platforms for eliminating pathological targets, remodeling diseased tissues, and coordinating local immune responses. Early clinical studies support their feasibility, but target recognition alone does not ensure sustained function after tissue entry. Recent advances in myeloid-adapted receptors, context-responsive circuits, checkpoint and metabolic engineering, in vivo mRNA delivery, and stem-cell-derived platforms have expanded the strategies available to improve tissue tracking, control cellular plasticity, and sustain effector capacity. Previous reviews have commonly organized the field by disease, target, or platform. Here, we examine engineered monocyte and macrophage therapies as integrated pharmacological systems structured across four coupled layers-sensing, signal integration, actuation, and delivery-and discuss how their coordination determines tissue exposure, functional durability, and pharmacodynamic readouts across therapeutic settings.

articles.title: Exploring the role of histone deacetylases and histone deacetylase inhibitors in obesity and emerging evidence from Anorexia Nervosa.
articles.abstract: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are key epigenetic regulators that modulate chromatin accessibility and transcriptional programs controlling metabolism, energy balance, and reward-related behaviors. Aberrant HDACs activity contributes to metabolic dysfunction by altering adipogenesis, thermogenic capacity, lipid profile, and hypothalamic circuits governing appetite. In obesity, specific HDAC isoforms promote adipocyte hypertrophy, impair browning of white adipose tissue, disrupt mitochondrial function, and exacerbate inflammation and insulin resistance. HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) counteract these effects by enhancing oxidative metabolism, stimulating thermogenesis, reducing adipocyte size, and improving systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis in preclinical models. Beyond peripheral metabolism, HDACi can also modulate neural pathways implicated in food intake, highlighting their potential influence in eating disorders, an area of research currently largely limited to anorexia nervosa. Research on HDACs, HDACi, and eating disorders is relatively recent; therefore, the characterization of potential molecular alterations and the identification of specific HDAC targets remain areas of ongoing development. Collectively, current evidence suggests that selective targeting of HDACs may offer a promising therapeutic strategy to correct epigenetic dysfunctions underlying both obesity and maladaptive feeding behaviors; however, translating these findings into clinical practice will require overcoming key challenges, including achieving isoform-specific selectivity, minimizing central nervous system-related side effects, and establishing efficacy and safety in human studies.

articles.title: Mitochondria-targeted drug delivery systems for aging-related diseases: Mechanisms, strategies, and advances.
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by increased oxidative stress, impaired energy metabolism, disrupted mitochondrial dynamics, abnormal quality control, and activation of apoptosis, represents a critical pathological basis for a wide range of aging-related diseases (ARDs), including neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, sarcopenia, and osteoarthritis. Mitochondria-targeted drug delivery systems increase the effective concentration of bioactive molecules within these dysfunctional organelles, offering novel strategies for the precise modulation of mitochondrial function. This review summarizes structural and functional changes in mitochondria during aging and their associations with major ARDs. We comprehensively review key advances in the design principles, mechanisms of action, and applications of passive targeting, stimuli-responsive systems, active targeting, and biomimetic drug delivery platforms. In addition, emerging interventions such as NAD+ supplementation, mitochondrial gene delivery, EV-mediated mitochondrial delivery and mitochondrial transplantation are discussed. Despite the demonstrated potential of these systems to restore mitochondrial homeostasis and tissue functionality in various disease models, their clinical translation remains constrained by obstacles including unstable targeting efficacy under pathological conditions, insufficient long-term safety of materials, manufacturing complexity, and a lack of standardized evaluation criteria. Future efforts should focus on integrating disease heterogeneity, advanced materials, and multi-omics technologies to advance mitochondria-targeted therapies toward standardization, individualization, and diagnostic-therapeutic integration.

articles.title: Nanomedicine strategies for overcoming cellular and microenvironmental barriers to cuproptosis-based cancer therapy.
articles.abstract: Cuproptosis, a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by mitochondrial proteotoxic stress, has emerged as a promising vulnerability for cancer therapy. However, its therapeutic translation is limited by cellular and microenvironmental barriers that restrict effective copper delivery, intracellular copper accumulation, mitochondrial engagement, and antitumor immune activation. This review summarizes the molecular basis of cuproptosis, including copper homeostasis, mitochondrial copper trafficking, lipoylated protein aggregation, and iron‑sulfur cluster disruption. We then examine how dysregulated copper transport, glutathione-mediated buffering, metabolic reprogramming, hypoxia, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments attenuate cuproptosis-based treatment. Focusing on these barriers, we discuss nanomedicine strategies designed to modulate copper homeostasis, deplete glutathione, reprogram tumor metabolism, alleviate hypoxia, and enhance antitumor immunity. These multifunctional platforms can enable tumor-selective copper delivery and spatiotemporally controlled activation while integrating complementary therapeutic modalities. Finally, we highlight unresolved challenges, including incomplete mechanistic understanding, tumor heterogeneity, insufficient real-time monitoring of cuproptosis, and the need to balance therapeutic efficacy with systemic copper toxicity. A systems-level integration of nanomedicine, mechanistic biology, and computational design may support the development of safer, more precise, and clinically actionable cuproptosis-based cancer therapies.

articles.title: Harnessing autophagy and its transcriptional regulation in tumorigenesis and neurodegeneration: Potential and existing therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process that maintains homeostasis by degrading and recycling cellular components. As autophagy is essential for metabolizing damaged organelles and toxic substances, it plays a crucial role in both normal physiology and pathological conditions. However, autophagy has dual roles in both tumorigenesis and neurodegeneration. In cancer, autophagy can act as a tumor suppressor by clearing damaged components in early stages, but promotes tumor survival and growth in later stages, particularly under stress. In neurodegeneration, impaired autophagy is implicated in the disease progression of conditions such as Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases, in which the failure to clear misfolded proteins and damaged organelles exacerbates disease pathology. This review is organized to cover the molecular machinery and transcriptional regulation of autophagy, its disease-specific subtypes, its dual roles in tumorigenesis and neurodegeneration, and the current pharmacological landscape for therapeutic targeting. Attention is given to pharmacological modulation of autophagy, including senolytic drugs that selectively eliminate senescent cells by exploiting their dependence on antiapoptotic survival pathways, and small-molecule regulators targeting key pathways such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase/Akt serine/threonine kinase/mechanistic target of rapamycin and AMP-activated protein kinase. Depending on the pathological context, these drugs are under development to either inhibit or induce autophagy. Additionally, we address the challenges and limitations in developing effective autophagy-targeting drugs, underscoring the need for further research to identify new compounds that can modulate cellular autophagic flux. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Autophagy is an important homeostatic mechanism, and its dysregulation contributes to a wide range of diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, a deeper mechanistic understanding of the regulation of autophagy is crucial for advancing targeted therapies with significant clinical impact.

articles.title: Role of PANoptosis in cancer: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic insights.
articles.abstract: Dysregulated cell death signaling profoundly influences oncogenesis, making the targeted elimination of malignant cells a cornerstone of modern oncological interventions. Insights into programmed cell death kinetics have revealed cross-talk among apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis, establishing the conceptual framework of PANoptosis. As an inflammatory death modality, PANoptosis is orchestrated by a multi-subunit protein platform termed the PANoptosome, which integrates and executes these distinct death programs. This review outlines the fundamental molecular cascades governing PANoptosis, alongside its multifaceted involvement in tumorigenesis, immune microenvironment remodeling, and metastatic dissemination. Although PANoptosis potentiates host antitumor defense mechanisms, its impact on malignant progression remains context-dependent. Pharmacological intervention directed at central node molecules or combined with radiation and immune checkpoint blockade represents a compelling strategy. Notably, suppressing ZBP1 attenuates chemotherapy-induced systemic toxicities, whereas multimodal therapies synergistically augment therapeutic efficacy. Nevertheless, precise regulatory networks demand further elucidation, and clinical translation requires rigorous validation. Ultimately, PANoptosis offers novel insights into cancer biology and paves the way for personalized therapeutic paradigms.

articles.title: Drug-Drug Interactions vs. Therapeutic Combinations in Patients with Congestive Heart Failure and Diabetes: An Ambispective Real-World Study.
articles.abstract: Concomitant congestive heart failure (CHF) and diabetes mellitus (DM) patients frequently are treated with polypharmacy, thus potentially increasing the risk of drug-drug interactions (pDDIs). Conventional DDI screening methods often fail to distinguish clinically significant interactions from recommended therapeutic combinations. This study assessed the prevalence, severity, and clinical consequences of pDDIs in hospitalized patients with CHF and DM. This ambispective, cross-sectional study included 144 hospitalized patients with CHF and DM. We used the Micromedex and Lexicomp databases to check prescriptions. We classified clinically relevant DDIs and therapeutic combinations requiring routine monitoring by severity. 207 pDDIs were identified, of which 84.1% were moderate and 15.9% severe. Polypharmacy was a major risk factor for the DDI burden, and over seven drugs were associated with significantly more interactions than fewer drugs (P < 0.001). Polypharmacy was an independent predictor of clinically significant DDI (AOR 3.42; 95% CI 1.78-6.59) in the multivariate analysis. The most commonly seen combinations (statin-ezetimibe and sulfonylurea-metformin therapy) are guideline-recommended and do not need to be avoided. Clinical pharmacists and prescribing clinicians performing context-aware interpretation of DDI alerts by differentiating between guideline-recommended therapeutic combinations requiring monitoring and truly actionable interactions can reduce alert fatigue, preserve evidence-based therapy, and support safe prescribing in complex CHF-DM patients.

articles.title: CRISPR screens identify ACSL4 as a key regulator in macrophage activation and metabolic inflammation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pro-inflammatory macrophages drive obesity-associated metabolic inflammation. Identifying key regulators of their activation is crucial for new therapies. This study aimed to identify novel regulators of pro-inflammatory adipose tissue macrophage (ATM) activation and assess their therapeutic potential. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We combined genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening with scRNA-seq data from human adipose tissue and identified long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 4 (ACSL4) as critical for pro-inflammatory ATM activation. Validation used myeloid-specific Acsl4 knockout mice (Acsl4fl/fl Lyz2Cre) and shRNA-mediated knockdown in macrophage cell lines (RAW264.7, THP-1, and iBMDM). Mechanisms were explored via mutagenesis, immunostaining, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and transcriptional activity assays. A high-throughput screen of 8,685 DrugBank compounds was performed to identify candidates targeting ACSL4. KEY RESULTS: ACSL4 deficiency markedly reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression (Tnfα, Il1β, and Il6). Myeloid ACSL4 deletion protected against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis, without affecting food intake, water intake, or locomotor activity in mice. However, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were not significantly affected. Mechanistically, ACSL4 contributed to inflammation independent of its enzymatic/ferroptotic functions (Thr328 mutation, troglitazone insensitivity). Instead, ACSL4 translocated to the nucleus in a karyopherin β1 (KPNB1)-dependent manner. DrugBank screening identified abemaciclib as a potential inhibitor of the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction. Notably, abemaciclib treatment reduced macrophage inflammation and attenuated HFD-induced obesity in mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: ACSL4 promotes pro-inflammatory macrophage activation through its KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation and cooperation with IRF5. Targeting the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic inflammation.

articles.title: SERINC3 promotes oral squamous cell carcinoma progression and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming involving c-MET/JNK/PGC-1α axis.
articles.abstract: Serine incorporator 3 (SERINC3) is a multi-transmembrane protein involved in membrane lipid biosynthesis but its role in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is undefined. Combining clinical specimens with public transcriptomic datasets, we found that SERINC3 was upregulated in OSCC tissues and that high expression was associated with poorer overall survival. Functionally, SERINC3 depletion impaired OSCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, whereas SERINC3 overexpression enhanced these phenotypes. In vivo, Serinc3 deletion suppressed 4NQO-induced oral tumorigenesis, and SERINC3 knockdown reduced tumor growth in both subcutaneous and patient-derived xenograft models. Mechanistically, SERINC3 sustained c-MET expression, and knockdown of either SERINC3 or MET increased JNK phosphorylation and PGC-1α levels; JNK inhibition with JNK-IN-8 partially reversed the phenotypic effects of SERINC3 depletion, while pharmacological PGC-1α activation with ZLN005 suppressed migration and invasion in vitro and xenograft growth in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing and metabolic assays further linked SERINC3 to mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. Together, these findings identify SERINC3 as a candidate driver of OSCC progression acting through c-MET/JNK/PGC-1α-associated signaling and mitochondrial metabolic regulation, and suggest it as a potential therapeutic target. The precise causal relationships within this signaling axis warrant further investigation.

articles.title: Low-dose Juglone Attenuates Pressure Overload-Induced Cardiac Hypertrophy through Lys207-dependent FoxO1 activation and Mitochondrial protection.
articles.abstract: Pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance. Here, we investigated the efficacy, safety window, and redox-regulatory mechanism of juglone, a naturally occurring 5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone. In mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC), high-dose juglone induced cardiac, hepatic, and renal toxicity, whereas 1mg/kg/day was well tolerated and attenuated cardiac hypertrophy. Juglone also suppressed Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and preserved mitochondrial ultrastructure and mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration, ATP production, and redox homeostasis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that juglone reduced stress-associated cardiomyocyte states and enriched calcium-handling cardiomyocytes. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, Biotin-Juglone pull-down assay, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assays, molecular docking, and mutational analyses identified FoxO1 as a functional target of juglone. Juglone engaged the FoxO1 DNA-binding domain in a Lys207-dependent manner, and was associated with FoxO1 deacetylation, nuclear accumulation, and transcriptional activation. Activated FoxO1 induced Sesn3 transcription and restored AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172. Sesn3 silencing markedly attenuated juglone-induced AMPK activation and impaired its protective effects against cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. FoxO1 silencing, FoxO1-K207Q mutation, blockade of FoxO1 deacetylation, or inhibition of FoxO1 transcriptional activity impaired these benefits. Importantly, myocardium from patients with aortic valve stenosis-associated hypertrophy exhibited increased FoxO1 acetylation, reduced cardiomyocyte nuclear FoxO1 localization, decreased Sesn3 expression and AMPK phosphorylation, and increased 4-HNE. Collectively, low-dose juglone attenuates pathological hypertrophy and preserves mitochondrial homeostasis through the FoxO1-Sesn3-AMPK axis, while highlighting the importance of dose-dependent redox effects in determining its therapeutic efficacy and systemic toxicity.

articles.title: A dual-gated engineered bacterial platform for spatiotemporally controlled precise protein degradation.
articles.abstract: Lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) have attracted much attention due to their ability to specifically target and degrade disease-related proteins on the cell membrane. However, their clinical application is limited by poor tumor specificity, systemic off-target effects, and a lack of temporal regulation. Engineered bacteria naturally home to tumors and serve as in situ production factories, but current approaches typically lack orthogonal regulation over payload release and functional activation, leading to premature exposure and suboptimal efficacy. Here, we develop a dual-gated engineered bacterial platform (DGTPB) that decouples LYTAC delivery from functional activation. Upon tumor colonization, DGTPB constitutively produces genetically encoded LYTACs, triggers their release via L-arabinose-induced bacterial lysis, and subsequently activates targeted degradation through red-light irradiation. This dual-gating design ensures high local LYTAC concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. We demonstrate that DGTPB-mediated degradation of EGFR and PD-L1 potently suppresses tumor growth and metastasis in both melanoma and breast cancer models. Owing to its modular architecture, DGTPB is readily reprogrammable against diverse disease-associated membrane proteins by simply exchanging targeting ligands. Collectively, DGTPB establishes a versatile, programmable, and safe framework for precision extracellular targeted protein degradation, thereby providing a new tool for engineered-bacteria-based platforms in cancer immunotherapy.

articles.title: Annexin A5-engineered nanovaccines synchronize spatiotemporal antigen release with phagocytosis checkpoint blockade for potent in situ cancer immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: In situ generation of autologous tumor vaccines from dying tumor cells offers a promising route for personalized cancer immunotherapy, yet is often limited by phosphatidylserine (PS)-mediated immunosuppressive clearance that can restrict downstream immune activation and favor M2-like macrophage polarization. Here, we report a sequentially orchestrated nanovaccine (NT@ANX5-P) that couples photodynamic therapy (PDT)-induced immunogenic tumor-cell damage with on-demand PS masking to enhance in situ tumor vaccination. The nanovaccine consists of a photosensitizer core cloaked with genetically engineered tumor cell membranes displaying Annexin A5 (ANX5) and further shielded by a ROS-cleavable PEG layer for circulatory shielding and local light-responsive activation. Upon localized light irradiation, tumor cells undergo PDT-induced damage and apoptosis, while ROS-triggered PEG cleavage increases ANX5 accessibility for binding exposed PS, thereby attenuating PS-dependent efferocytic clearance and favoring progression toward secondary necrosis. This coordinated treatment enhanced dendritic cell maturation, remodeled tumor-associated macrophage phenotypes, and increased T-cell responses. In 4T1 tumor-bearing mice, NT@ANX5-P suppressed primary and distant tumor growth, reduced lung metastasis, and induced protection against homologous tumor rechallenge. CD8+ T-cell depletion markedly weakened bilateral tumor control, supporting an important functional contribution of CD8+ T cells. These findings provide proof-of-concept for coordinating PDT-induced antigen generation with spatially regulated modulation of PS-dependent dying-cell clearance in the 4T1 model.

articles.title: Decoding extracellular vesicle-biomolecule interactions: How the biomolecular corona shapes extracellular vesicle biodistribution and clearance in vivo.
articles.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising endogenous nanocarriers, yet how biomolecules adsorption shapes their in vivo fate remains unclear. Here, we examine how biomolecular corona formation regulates the biodistribution, cellular recognition, and clearance of extracellular vesicles. Using EVs derived from macrophages and breast cancer cells, together with artificially prepared cell membrane-derived vesicles (CVs) generated from the corresponding parental cells as controls, we observed markedly different circulation and clearance behaviors despite their comparable physicochemical properties. Proteomic analyses revealed distinct and extensive biomolecular adsorption profiles on EVs compared with their corresponding CVs. In vivo imaging shows that EVs undergo faster systemic clearance and preferential accumulation in the liver and spleen. Cellular-level analyses identify Kupffer cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, splenic macrophages, and circulating innate immune cells-especially neutrophils-as key mediators of EVs clearance. In vitro studies further confirm that biomolecular corona formation enhances immune recognition and uptake, with EVs consistently showing higher phagocytosis than CVs. Notably, opsonin proteins such as complement C3 and immunoglobulins are enriched on EVs surfaces and strongly correlate with increased macrophage uptake. Overall, these results highlight biomolecular corona formation as a critical determinant of EVs biological identity and in vivo fate.

articles.title: Advancing biopharmaceutics modelling of extended-release formulations with sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 biorelevant upper GI and colonic dissolution.
articles.abstract: Predicting the in vivo performance of extended-release (ER) products is difficult because drug release is excipient-controlled and may continue into the colon, a region poorly represented by conventional dissolution methods. Here, during ER formulation development, a biorelevant in vitro-in silico workflow was established to support formulation development of rocavorexant, a weakly water-soluble, high-permeability BCS II compound formulated as a HPMC-matrix ER tablet. Formulations were screened for food effect risk using the dynamic in vitro TIM-1 gastrointestinal model, before dissolution profiles measured in sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 upper-GI and colonic transit were used as dissolution input for PBBM. TIM-derived dissolution profiles were constructed from luminal samples, distinguishing apparently dissolved from dispersed drug, and from filtrate/dialysate fractions from the jejunal, ileal and colonic compartments representing dissolved drug removed from the systems. PBBM using conventional USP-I dissolution, either directly or after level A IVIVC transformation, failed to reproduce clinical pharmacokinetics, underpredicting early exposure and missing a late 20-24 h plasma plateau. Sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 input predicted clinical exposure well (predicted/observed Cmax 1.03; AUC 0.91-0.94), recovered the plateau and linked regional release, solubilisation, absorption and systemic pharmacokinetics.

articles.title: Investigation of the mechanisms and modulation of irinotecan-induced emesis in Suncus murinus.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Irinotecan is a widely used chemotherapeutic agent that frequently causes nausea and emesis. Its emetic mechanism of action is poorly understood and the choice of drugs to reduce nausea and emesis is largely empirical. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Using Suncus murinus, we examined (i) the dose-response and temporal profile of irinotecan-induced emesis; (ii) emetic potential of its active metabolite, SN-38; (iii) involvement of vagal and central pathways; (iv) efficacies of classical antiemetics administered alone, or in combinations. Behavioural, respiratory, metabolic and c-Fos immunohistochemical analyses were used to delineate mechanisms involved in emesis control. A microelectrode array (MEA) system assessed the effects of irinotecan and SN-38 on gastrointestinal slow-wave activity. KEY RESULTS: Irinotecan induced dose-dependent emesis within 24 h, whereas SN-38 was inactive. Neither compound altered respiration. Bilateral abdominal vagotomy attenuated early-phase (0-4 h) of irinotecan-induced emesis. Palonosetron suppressed emesis and was the most effective monotherapy; olanzapine alone also showed antiemetic efficacy. Notably, olanzapine-containing combinations with palonosetron and aprepitant or dexamethasone provided superior protection compared with monotherapies. Irinotecan increased c-Fos expression in the brainstem, and hypothalamic and limbic regions; palonosetron selectively reduced brainstem activation. Serum metabolomics revealed reduced tyramine levels and associations between emetic episodes and 5-HT-related pathways. MEA recordings showed that irinotecan, but not SN-38, produced selective disruptions of upper-gut rhythmic activity. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Irinotecan-induced emesis is mediated predominantly through 5-HT₃-dependent vagal-brainstem pathways with additional activation of hypothalamic and limbic regions. Altered intestinal pacemaker activity and 5-HT metabolism may contribute to gastrointestinal adverse effects.

articles.title: Toward a Platform PBPK Model to Characterize the Plasma and Tissue Disposition of Unconjugated Antisense Oligonucleotides and GalNAc-Conjugated Small Interfering RNAs in Preclinical Species and Human.
articles.abstract: Unconjugated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as transformative therapeutic modalities, but their translation remains hindered by complex pharmacokinetics characterized by rapid plasma clearance, heterogeneous tissue uptake, and prolonged intracellular retention. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling offers a mechanistic framework to integrate these processes across species, yet applications to oligonucleotides remain limited, and existing efforts are typically restricted to specific chemistries or routes of administration. This study aimed to develop a cross-species PBPK platform to characterize the plasma and tissue disposition of unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-siRNAs in preclinical species and humans, and to evaluate the consistency of estimated drug-specific parameters with pre-specified allometric scaling relationships within the domain of compounds and routes considered. Published datasets spanning mice, rats, non-human primates, and humans were integrated for representative unconjugated ASOs (Malat-1, GluR1, p-tau, tominersen) and GalNAc-siRNAs (ALN-AT3, givosiran, fitusiran). The PBPK model incorporated 11 tissue compartments, cerebrospinal fluid substructures, tissue substructures, endosomal trafficking, non-specific binding in kidney and liver, and ASGPR-mediated internalization for GalNAc-siRNAs. Parameters for endocytosis, exocytosis, and degradation were estimated, and estimated values were compared with pre-specified allometric exponents to assess physiological plausibility (i.e., as a consistency check rather than independent inference of scaling laws). The model captured plasma, liver, kidney, and CNS profiles across species, reproducing rapid systemic clearance with prolonged tissue half-lives. Estimated parameter values for endocytosis, exocytosis, and non-specific kidney binding were consistent with pre-specified allometric exponents (b = -0.25 and -0.2, respectively), supporting the physiological plausibility of the estimates. Sensitivity analyses identified endocytosis and rate of degradation as dominant determinants of systemic and tissue disposition. This work establishes a translational PBPK platform for unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-conjugated siRNAs, enabling quantitative interspecies extrapolation within the domain of the compounds, routes, and species studied. The framework provides a mechanistic basis to support dose selection, safety assessment, and clinical translation for these subclasses; extrapolation to other oligonucleotide subclasses (e.g., GalNAc-ASOs, unconjugated siRNAs, LNP-formulated oligonucleotides) will require additional datasets and dedicated validation.

articles.title: A PTPRO inhibitor Pi mitigates endotoxemia-induced encephalopathy-mediated blood-brain barrier disruption through cytoskeletal regulation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Septic encephalopathy (SE) is closely associated with disruption of blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in neurological deficits and poor clinical outcomes. Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) regulates disease states by dephosphorylating membrane-associated proteins and modulating intracellular signalling. Here we have examined the role of PTPRO in regulating BBB permeability and have assessed a PTPRO inhibitor (Pi) in mitigating BBB disruption during endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Genetic and pharmacological approaches, including PTPRO overexpression, knockdown or deficiency and Pi treatment, were used to evaluate endothelial dysfunction in bEND.3 cells, primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and an LPS-induced murine model of endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. Barrier dysfunction, cytoskeletal remodelling and signalling events were assessed using permeability assays, immunoblotting, immunofluorescence and in vivo BBB leakage analyses. KEY RESULTS: LPS increased PTPRO expression in brain tissue from endotoxemic mice and cerebral endothelial cells. Elevated PTPRO promoted F-actin reorganization, stress fibre formation and intercellular gap formation, whereas Pi treatment or PTPRO silencing attenuated these changes. PTPRO overexpression worsened endothelial barrier dysfunction, while Pi reduced thrombin-induced permeability in bEND.3 cells and wild-type primary endothelial cells. Primary endothelial cells from PTPRO-deficient mice were protected. Mechanistically, PTPRO regulated cytoskeletal dynamics through the ErbB2-Rho-MLC2 pathway. In vivo, Pi treatment and PTPRO deficiency reduced BBB leakage, with limited effects on inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: These findings identify PTPRO as an important regulator of BBB disruption in endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy and support pharmacological targeting of PTPRO as a potential strategy for preserving sepsis-associated BBB injury.

articles.title: N-nitroso-hydrochlorothiazide: in vivo mutagenicity evaluation in a transgenic rodent model.
articles.abstract: N-nitrosamine drug substance related impurities (NDSRIs) are considered to be within the "cohort of concern" (CoC) due to their potential mutagenic carcinogenicity. However, increasing evidence indicates variability in mutagenic potency across this class. N-nitroso-hydrochlorothiazide (N-nitroso-HCTZ), an impurity associated with hydrochlorothiazide, has shown positive results in bacterial mutagenicity (Ames) assays, although mechanistic studies suggest these findings are likely driven by reactive degradation products rather than the parent compound. To further characterize mutagenic potential in vivo, a transgenic rodent (TGR) gene mutation assay was conducted in the Muta™Mouse test system. Male mice were administered N-nitroso-HCTZ by oral gavage at 0, 18.5, 55.7, 167, 500, or 750 mg/kg/day for 28 consecutive days. Mutant frequency (lacZ) was evaluated in liver and glandular stomach at 167, 500, and 750 mg/kg/day. Systemic exposure was confirmed in a toxicokinetic study following a single 750 mg/kg dose. N-nitroso-HCTZ was well tolerated, and no statistically significant increases in mutant frequency were observed in either tissue at any evaluated dose. All values were within historical control ranges, while the positive control demonstrated the anticipated response. Under the conditions of this study, N-nitroso-HCTZ did not induce gene mutations in vivo.

articles.title: One year of Commissioner's National Priority Vouchers.
New Approach Methodologies (NAMs): Guiding Clinical Predictions through Human-Relevant Evidence.
Aquilaria Leaves (Thymelaeaceae): A Comprehensive Review of Ethnobotany, Traditional Applications, Phytochemistry, Pharmacological Activities, Toxicity and Quality Evaluation.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Aquilaria species are well known for agarwood, while their leaves are also used in regional folk medicine and consumed as herbal teas in southern China and Southeast Asia, mainly for inflammatory conditions, infections, and stress-related symptoms. AIMS OF THE REVIEW: This review summarizes the ethnobotany, taxonomy, traditional applications, phytochemistry, pharmacology, toxicity and quality evaluation of Aquilaria leaves, and identifies gaps that warrant further investigation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Relevant literature was collected from Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, PubMed, CNKI, and Wan Fang Data, including journal articles, books, and dissertations. Flora of China and Plants of the World Online were consulted to verify species distribution and accepted botanical names. Chemical structures were drawn using ChemDraw 22.0.0. RESULTS: A total of 185 compounds have been recorded from Aquilaria leaves. Phytochemical and pharmacological studies mainly involve three species, A. sinensis, A. crassna, and A. malaccensis. The major compound classes include flavonoids, terpenoids, benzophenones, organic acids, xanthones, and 2-(2-phenylethyl)chromones, with flavonoids (39) and terpenoids (43) predominating. Pharmacological studies have largely focused on crude extracts, with relatively few investigations of isolated compounds, and have demonstrated anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antibacterial, antidiabetic, laxative, and neuroprotective activities. Available toxicological studies generally indicate low acute toxicity within the tested dose ranges, although evidence on long-term safety remains limited. Quality evaluation has mainly relied on chromatographic profiling and multi-component determination, while standardized quality criteria remain to be established. CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights Aquilaria leaves as a renewable and underexplored medicinal resource by integrating evidence from traditional applications, phytochemistry, pharmacology, toxicity, and quality evaluation. However, current evidence is still limited by crude-extract-based studies, insufficient active-constituent characterization, and limited long-term safety and clinical data. Further research is needed to identify the active constituents, elucidate their underlying mechanisms, and establish standardized quality control and safety evaluation systems for the safe and effective use of Aquilaria leaves.

articles.title: Monocarboxylate transporters 1 and 4 in tumor lactate exchange: Molecular mechanisms, pharmacological inhibition, and therapeutic translation.
articles.abstract: Lactate is no longer viewed merely as a glycolytic end product but as a metabolic substrate and signaling molecule that promotes tumor growth, metabolic cooperation, extracellular acidification, immune suppression, and treatment resistance. Monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) supports gradient-dependent lactate uptake or efflux, whereas monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4) sustains lactate-proton export from hypoxic glycolytic cells, together coordinating intratumoral lactate exchange and pH homeostasis. However, an integrated framework is still lacking to distinguish transporter expression from functional lactate dependence and to connect mechanistic insights with cancer-specific pharmacological evidence. This review integrates the molecular architecture, proton-coupled transport mechanisms, substrate recognition, and chaperone-dependent trafficking of MCT1 and MCT4, and explains how their spatially distinct functions shape metabolic compartmentalization and tumor microenvironment remodeling. It further examines cancer-type-specific dependencies and distinguishes simple expression associations from experimentally supported reliance on lactate transport, with attention to extracellular acidification, angiogenesis, immune suppression, stromal remodeling, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. MCT-directed agents are systematically classified as nonselective, MCT1-selective, MCT4-selective, or dual/multi-isoform inhibitors and critically evaluated according to potency, selectivity, structural support, cellular target engagement, in vivo efficacy, resistance mechanisms, pharmacokinetics, safety, and clinical maturity. These data are integrated into a translational framework that separates transporter expression, functional lactate-transport dependence, pharmacological target engagement, and metabolic escape. Overall, actionable MCT dependence should be defined by membrane localization, lactate flux, limited compensatory capacity, and demonstrable target engagement rather than by transporter abundance alone, thereby informing biomarker-guided combinations and next-generation MCT-directed therapy.

articles.title: Overcoming drug delivery barriers to Unlock the therapeutic potential of conventional chemotherapy in glioblastoma.
articles.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most incurable malignancies, and systemic therapies continue to provide only limited clinical benefit despite encouraging preclinical evidence. Therapeutic failure has traditionally been attributed to insufficient drug efficacy or intrinsic resistance mechanisms. However, increasing evidence suggests that many conventional chemotherapeutic agents retain substantial antitumor activity but fail to achieve sufficient intratumoral exposure because of delivery barriers. This review proposes that inadequate drug delivery represents a major barrier limiting the therapeutic efficacy of conventional chemotherapeutics in GBM, independent of their intrinsic pharmacodynamic activity. We re-evaluate conventional chemotherapeutic agents, including alkylating agents, microtubule-targeting agents, topoisomerase inhibitors, and platinum compounds, from the perspective of blood-brain barrier (BBB) transport, heterogeneous intratumoral drug distribution, and dose-limiting systemic toxicity. We further discuss how emerging drug delivery strategies can restore the therapeutic potential of these agents by improving brain penetration and intratumoral distribution without altering their intrinsic pharmacological properties.By reframing chemotherapy failure in GBM as a consequence of both pharmacodynamic resistance and inadequate drug delivery, this Review highlights drug delivery as an underappreciated determinant of therapeutic efficacy.

articles.title: Circadian system and human health: From molecular mechanisms to clinical integration.
articles.abstract: The circadian system, an evolutionarily conserved endogenous oscillator coordinating physiological adaptation to geophysical cycles, coordinates hierarchical gene regulatory networks, metabolic pathways, and physiological functions to maintain organismal homeostasis. Circadian disturbances caused by modern lifestyle are recognized as key etiological factors in complex multisystem disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, and oncogenic pathologies. The review synthesizes current evidence to delineate that organ-specific physiological programs across the human body are under circadian clock, and chronic desynchronization of system drives a broad spectrum of clinical disorders. Moreover, the review critically assesses state-of-the-art therapeutic modalities, and identifies promising technological innovations. It advances precision chronomedicine by proposing public health interventions, such as environmental modification combined with behavioral education, offering a roadmap for clinical implementation of circadian restoration therapies.

articles.title: Overcoming the nuclear barrier in nonviral gene therapy: mechanisms, carrier design, and translational perspectives on NLS peptide and DNA targeting sequence strategies.
articles.abstract: Efficient delivery of plasmid DNA (pDNA) into the nucleus remains a major bottleneck in nonviral gene therapy, particularly in post-mitotic and slowly dividing cells where the nuclear envelope constitutes a permanent barrier to passive entry. This review considers the two main strategies for active nuclear targeting: nuclear localisation signal (NLS) peptides, which recruit importin-α/β receptors directly to DNA cargo, and DNA nuclear targeting sequences (DTS), which exploit NLS-bearing transcription factors to mediate piggyback nuclear import. Rather than re-cataloguing nuclear import biology, we focus on the conditions under which each strategy succeeds or fails, incorporating advances in nuclear pore complex architecture and permeability, karyopherin-FG-nucleoporin electrostatics, and cytoplasmic constraints such as barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF)-mediated clustering of exogenous DNA. NLS classes are compared with universal (SV40 enhancer), inducible (NF-κB) and tissue-specific (SMGA, SP-C, T1α) DTS elements, and four chemical coupling strategies are evaluated across peptide-, polymer- and lipid-based nanoassemblies. To address the near-absence of NLS/DTS mechanisms in current clinical pDNA programmes, we propose the Nuclear Accessibility Index (NAI): a three-axis framework integrating cell division status, carrier-DNA accessibility and intracellular signalling context. Treating the NAI as an axis vector rather than a summed score defines permissive, conditional and excluded regions of the design space. Two matter in practice: one in which highly proliferative cells render active targeting redundant, and one in which the rate-limiting problem is carrier engineering rather than the addition of a signal. The NAI offers design principles for nuclear-targeted nanocarriers and defines the preconditions for therapeutically relevant active import.

articles.title: Identification of a novel Microbacterium species and biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles: activation of apoptosis and dysregulation of ABCG transporters in gastric adenocarcinoma cells.
articles.abstract: Gastric cancer has high morbidity and mortality rates worldwide, often requiring new therapeutic approaches. Biosynthesis of gold nanoparticles (GNPs) offers a promising treatment due to their unique biological properties and biocompatibility. In this study, we synthesized gold nanoparticles using the cultural supernatant of Microbacterium sp. MAH-37 (MM37-S) and evaluated their anti-gastric cancer activity, focusing on apoptosis induction and regulation of the ABCG transporter pathway. The Microbacterium sp. strain MAH-37 was isolated from pumpkin garden soil, and its morphology was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The successful biosynthesis of MM37-S-GNP was confirmed by UV-visible spectroscopy, SAED, DLS, FTIR, XRD, EDX, and FE-TEM analyses. Biological evaluations revealed that MM37-S-GNPs exhibited cytotoxicity of approximately 72% at 200 µg/mL against AGS cells and confirmed by colony formation and Live/Dead assay, whereas normal HFE-145 cells was non-toxic. Furthermore, Hoechst 33,258, propidium iodide, and Mito Tracker revealed nuclear condensation and fragmentation, membrane-compromised cells, and mitochondrial disruption, respectively, indicating cell death via apoptosis. H2DCFDA staining demonstrated a significant increase intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in AGS cells following MM37-S-GNP. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that treatment induced apoptosis in AGS cells, with 30.4% apoptotic cells observed at 200 µg/mL. Consistently, mRNA and protein expression levels confirmed apoptosis cell death, as evidenced by an increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and elevated levels of cleaved caspase-9. Additionally, Western blot analysis revealed that treatment with higher doses of MM37-S-GNPs significantly downregulated the expression of ABCG1 and ABCG2 transporters. MM37-S-GNPs selectivelyeliminated gastric cancer cells through ROS-mediated mitochondrial damage and apoptotic pathways, while effectively regulating ABCG transporter expression, highlighting their potential as a promising nanotherapeutic agent.

articles.title: Combined antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation against multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium.
articles.abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecium has created an urgent need for alternative antimicrobial strategies capable of overcoming conventional antibiotic resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. In the present study, the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite, a sunflower oil-based nanoemulsion, and their combined formulation were evaluated against both a clinical MDR isolate and the reference strain E. faecium MCC 2763. The prepared formulations were characterized using dynamic light scattering (DLS), zeta potential analysis, and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Antibacterial activity was assessed by minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), time-kill kinetics, impedance-based growth monitoring, bacterial adherence assays, and biofilm inhibition studies. The combined nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation showed greater antibacterial and antibiofilm activity than the individual formulations under the experimental conditions evaluated. Time-kill and biofilm assays indicated improved inhibition of bacterial growth and biofilm formation, while impedance measurements further supported the antibacterial activity of the combined formulation. Although the present findings demonstrate the promising antibacterial potential of the developed formulation, formal synergy analysis, cytotoxicity evaluation, advanced physicochemical characterization, and mechanistic investigations were beyond the scope of this study. These investigations will be essential in future work to further evaluate the therapeutic potential of this formulation. Overall, the developed Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation represents a promising antibacterial platform for combating multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium and warrants further investigation through comprehensive preclinical evaluation.

articles.title: PVA/chitosan-based hydrogels integrated with tilapia skin-derived collagen and Urtica dioica offers a promising approach for effective burn wound healing via transcriptional modulation of bFgf, Mmp2, Jak/Stat3, and α-Sma signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Cutaneous wound repair is governed by a highly coordinated physiological cascade that includes recruitment of inflammatory cells, release of cytokine mediators, deposition of extracellular matrix components, and subsequent remodeling of scar tissue. Nowadays, plant extracts are viewed as an efficient alternative for wound healing. Urtica dioica (U. dioica) is rich in diverse bioactive plant compounds with varied therapeutic effects and appears to support skin wound repair. However, the molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways through which they influence regenerating tissues and cells remain poorly understood. This study aimed to confirm the signaling cascade and mechanism of topical application of a hydrogel formulation incorporated with tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus L.) skin-derived collagen and U. dioica extract on the skin regeneration process based on histopathological, TEM assessment as well as analyze alterations in the expression of key wound healing-related genes, such as Jak/Stat3, Smad3, fibroblast growth factor 2 (fgf2) genes, Acta2 ( α smooth muscle actin), and matrix metalloproteinases (Mmp2) gene in rat burn model. UPLC-ESI-MS/MS also analyzed the chemical composition of U. dioica. Thirty-five animals were randomly allocated to seven groups (n = 5 per group): negative control (NCtrl; no treatment), positive control (PCtrl), hydrogel base treated group (Hgb G), tilapia collagen hydrogel (ColHgb G), MEBO® cream (MEBO G), U. dioica extract (UD G), and a combination of collagen hydrogel plus U. dioica extract (ColHgb-UD G). Burn wound (2 × 2 cm) were made on the back of each generally anaesthetized rat, and wound surface area was measured on days 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 post-burn. The animals were then sacrificed, and tissues were collected for histological, TEM, and molecular analysis. Our results showed that the methanolic extract of the aerial parts of Urtica dioica was predominantly composed of flavonoids and fatty acids. Analysis in the negative ionization mode enabled the identification of several flavonoids, including apigenin, isorhamnetin, taxifolin, and eriodictyol, detected in both free and glycosylated forms. Wound closure was faster in the ColHgb-UD group than in the control-positive group. Gene expression patterns showed that U. dioica-treated rats, either alone or mixed with collagen hydrogel, notably inhibited the expression of profibrotic factors Jack/Stat3 and Acta2, while activating angiogenesis Fbgf2, Smad3 as well as Mmp2 compared with the positive control group. The histopathological findings showed significant healing progress in the ColHgb-UD group compared with the positive control untreated group and the other treated groups. Results demonstrate superior wound healing performance for ColHgb-UD compared to the control positive group the synergistic effect of U. dioica and collagen showed less scarring, more blood capillaries, less inflammatory cells therefore remarkably healed faster making the extract ideal for wound healing applications and a novel drug candidate for wound healing.

articles.title: The dual role of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis in glial cell survival and neuroinflammation.
articles.abstract: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by a triad of inflammation, demyelination, and neurodegeneration, yet current disease-modifying therapies are limited in their ability to halt progressive neurodegeneration or promote remyelination. The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway is a master regulator of these divergent cellular processes and therefore represents a biological paradox in multiple sclerosis. In the pathogenic facet of the disease, activation of this axis supports the differentiation and effector functions of pro-inflammatory T- and B-cells and contributes to inflammatory programs in microglia and macrophages. In the regenerative facet, physiological PI3K/AKT/mTOR activity is required for oligodendrocyte precursor-cell survival, differentiation, myelin synthesis, and maintenance of myelin integrity. Astrocytic signaling adds another layer of context-dependence, with pathway activity influencing reactive gliosis and the inflammatory or reparative properties of the lesion environment. Consequently, systemic inhibition of the pathway may suppress neuroinflammation while simultaneously interfering with endogenous repair. This review therefore considers PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis according to these opposing pathogenic and protective functions, highlighting the importance of cell type, disease stage, and treatment timing. Precision strategies capable of selectively suppressing inflammatory signaling while preserving or restoring pro-regenerative activity, potentially through cell-specific molecular targets, may provide a more rational therapeutic approach than generalized pathway inhibition.

articles.title: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol ameliorates oxidative stress, mitochondrial redox state, and neuroinflammation induced by high-fructose diet.
articles.abstract: This study investigates the effects of a high-fructose diet (HFD) on brain oxidative stress, mitochondrial redox state, and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, and specifically evaluates whether delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) attenuates these HFD-induced changes. Thirty-two Sprague-Dawley rats were divided into four groups: Control, HFD (10% fructose in drinking water for 12 weeks), THC (1.5 mg/kg daily for the last 4 weeks), and HFD + THC (HFD for 12 weeks with THC co-administration during the final 4 weeks). Biochemical biomarkers (AOPP, DT, KYN, MDA, AGE, T-SH, NADH, FAD, serotonin, insulin) and mRNA expression levels of inflammation-related genes (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, NF-κB) were analyzed in brain tissues. The HFD significantly increased levels of protein oxidation (AOPP, DT, KYN, AGE); lipid peroxidation (MDA); and NADH and FAD fluorescence whilst decreasing total thiol (T-SH) content. HFD also increased the mRNA expression of all inflammatory markers examined. In contrast, THC treatment significantly reduced oxidative damage and NADH and FAD fluorescence and reduced the relative mRNA expression of the investigated inflammation-related genes. Strong positive correlations were observed between pro-inflammatory cytokine mRNA expression and oxidative stress markers. HFD causes significant biochemical and molecular damage to the brain. THC administration was associated with a significant attenuation of HFD-induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial redox state, and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, suggesting that it may mitigate diet-associated neurochemical perturbations.

articles.title: Comparative hepatoprotective effects of Ginkgo biloba extract and N-Acetylcysteine against methotrexate-induced liver injury in rats: modulation of IκB-α, p38 MAPK, and p53 phosphorylation.
articles.abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) is an effective chemotherapeutic agent whose use can be limited by hepatotoxicity. This study comparatively evaluated the effects of Ginkgo biloba extract (GbE) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) on MTX-induced liver injury, focusing on oxidative stress, inflammatory and apoptotic responses, and associated hepatic phosphorylation of Inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B alpha (IκB-α), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK), and tumor protein p53 (p53), key components of stress-responsive signaling pathways. Thirty-two adult male rats were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 8/group). MTX (20 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered once on Day 4. GbE or NAC (200 mg/kg, p.o.) was administered for 3 days before and 6 days after MTX exposure. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total and direct bilirubin and hepatic malondialdehyde (MDA), nitric oxide (NO), reduced glutathione (GSH), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), tumor necrosis factor- alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), Bcl-2-associated X protein (Bax), and B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) were assessed. Hepatic phosphorylation of IκBα, p38 MAPK, and p53 was evaluated by Western blotting. MTX significantly (P < 0.001) increased serum ALT by 120% and hepatic MDA, TNF-α, IL-1β and Bax by 127%, 386%, 163%, and 439%, respectively, while reducing GSH and Bcl-2 by 66% and 63%, relative to control. Phosphorylation of IκBα, p38 MAPK, and p53 increased by 35%, 64%, and 68%, respectively. GbE and NAC significantly (P < 0.001) attenuated these alterations, with NAC producing generally greater effects than GbE. GbE and NAC attenuated MTX-induced hepatic injury across interconnected oxidative, inflammatory, apoptotic, and signaling endpoints. NAC showed a generally stronger response under the conditions tested. These findings support further investigation of both agents as potential strategies for mitigating MTX-associated hepatotoxicity.

articles.title: Chemogenetic inhibition of the ventrolateral orbitofrontal cortex disrupts novelty-guided updating of spatial memories and alters hippocampal engram reactivation.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Adaptive behavior requires revising memories when outcomes deviate from expectations. The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is implicated in representing outcome expectancies, but its role in memory-updating, beyond value-based learning, remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: We tested whether the ventrolateral OFC (VLO) contributes to hippocampal-dependent memory-updating in the Objects in Updated Locations (OUL) task, where novelty-driven exploration provides a behavioral readout consistent with successful updating of spatial information. METHODS: Using inhibitory DREADDs, in male and female (Swiss Webster and C57BL/6) mice, we suppressed VLO activity during the Updating session, when new object-location information was introduced. RESULTS: Control mice preferentially explored the updated object-location configuration during Updating and discriminated between updated and novel object-location configurations at Test, whereas VLO-inhibited mice did not. VLO inhibition when no updating demand was present did not alter exploration of novel object-location configurations or memory for the original spatial configuration at Test. CONCLUSIONS: These results indicate that VLO activity is selectively required when novelty must be interpreted relative to prior experience, implicating this region in evaluating change rather than detecting it. To assess hippocampal ensemble dynamics, we tagged neuronal ensembles, in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) recruited during Updating, followed by quantification of overlap between Updating-tagged cells and ensembles reactivated at Test. We found that VLO inhibition reduced reactivation of Updating-tagged dDG ensembles, paralleling the behavioral impairments observed in the OUL task. These findings support a role for the VLO in hippocampal-dependent memory-updating and extend OFC models beyond reward contexts to include predictive updating of spatial memory representations. CLINICAL TRIAL: Not applicable.

articles.title: Systematic review of clinical trials and cohort studies evaluating HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens to inform updated Canadian guidelines.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: We conducted a systematic review of clinical trials and cohort studies on HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens to inform updated 2025 Canadian guidelines. METHODS: We searched Medline and Embase (July 2017-June 2024) for studies reporting on: HIV acquisition, PEP completion, adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation and/or moderate to severe adverse events. Two reviewers independently screened abstracts and publications and extracted data from eligible articles. RESULTS: Of 5226 abstracts screened, we retrieved 112 full-text articles and included 22. Median study size was 160 (range = 52-26 988) participants. Regimens included DTG + TDF/XTC (n = 4, 18%), EVG/c/TDF/FTC (n = 4, 18%), BIC/TAF/FTC (n = 4, 18%), RAL + TDF/FTC (n = 4, 18%), EVG/c/TAF/FTC (n = 3, 14%), RPV/TDF/FTC (n = 2, 9%), DOR/TDF/FTC (n = 2, 9%), MVC + TDF/FTC (n = 1, 5%), a wide variety of protease inhibitor-based regimens (n = 7, 32%) and novel combinations with the injectable fusion inhibitor albuvirtide (n = 1, 5%); a third of studies included three or more regimens (n = 8, 36%). Among studies examining PEP completion rates (n = 12, 55%), cumulative completion rate was 86.6% (7779/8983 PEP episodes) and appeared highest for RAL + TDF/FTC, BIC/FTC/TAF and DOR/TDF/3TC at 96.4%, 96.3% and 95.0%, respectively. PEP tolerability was good, with few discontinuations due to adverse events; where data were available, this was lowest for INSTI-based regimens at 0.5% (pooled across two studies) for RAL + TDF/FTC, 1.0% (1/99) for DTG + TDF/XTC, 1.8% (2/109) for BIC/TAF/FTC and zero with albuvirtide (0/198). HIV seroconversions were rare (n = 5/8134, 0.06%) and often related to premature PEP discontinuation or repeated exposures. CONCLUSIONS: Multiple PEP regimens have been associated with high completion, good tolerability and rare seroconversion, supporting their inclusion in clinical guidelines.

articles.title: zDHHC11 is a Common Palmitoyltransferase Regulating Microglia-Mediated Neuroinflammation across Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is a shared feature across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and diabetic cognitive impairment (DCI), but the convergent molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated whether protein S-palmitoylation serves as a common regulator of microglial neuroinflammation across distinct neurodegenerative diseases etiologies and aimed to identify the key palmitoyltransferase involved. METHODS: In vivo ND models (APP/PS1 for AD, MPTP for PD, STZ/high-fat diet for DCI) and in vitro BV2 microglial models stimulated with amyloid-β (Aβ), lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or high glucose (HG) were established. Microglial morphology, inflammatory responses, and the TLR4/MyD88 pathway were assessed by immunofluorescence, RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and ELISA. Protein palmitoylation levels were evaluated using 2-BP and ABE assays. Palmitoyltransferase expression profiling was performed, and protein-level validation was conducted both in vitro and in vivo. Subsequently, the identified common enzyme, zDHHC11, was knocked down by siRNA to determine its functional role. RESULTS: All three ND models showed robust microglial activation with a pro-inflammatory amoeboid morphology. Aβ, LPS, and HG each upregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines and activated the TLR4/MyD88 pathway in BV2 cells. Palmitoylation inhibition with 2-BP attenuated cytokine production, and all three stimuli increased total protein palmitoylation. Among all palmitoyltransferases screened, zDHHC11 was uniquely and consistently upregulated by all three stimuli. This upregulation was further corroborated at the protein level, with elevated zDHHC11 expression observed both in cultured cells and in brain tissue sections. Knockdown of Zdhhc11 suppressed cytokine expression/secretion and reduced TLR4/MyD88 levels, indicating that zDHHC11 acts upstream of this common pathway. CONCLUSION: Protein S-palmitoylation mediated by zDHHC11 is a convergent mechanism driving microglial pro-inflammatory activation across distinct ND etiologies. zDHHC11 represents a common regulator of TLR4/MyD88-dependent neuroinflammation and a potential therapeutic target for multiple NDs.

articles.title: Of mice and little humans: A comparison of the issues facing drug delivery to wildlife and pediatric patients.
articles.abstract: Despite them being two very different patient populations, wildlife and pediatrics share many of the same challenges when it comes to drug development, delivery and the regulatory and clinical factors that impact on development of effective medicines. Drug delivery to wildlife species for prevention and treatment of disease, for conservation or pest control, is an emerging field of research. The current global H5N1 avian flu outbreaks has highlighted zoonotic disease and made us acutely aware of the important link between human health and wildlife health, however effective treatment of wildlife faces significant practical challenges and a paucity of quantitative data. Pediatric patients are also disadvantaged under current development paradigms, in part through ethical hurdles, but also through biopharmaceutical and clinical practice complications. Here, we provide a comparison of the challenges faced with the development of oral formulations for pediatric and wildlife patients and identify areas of translation from one field to the other that can benefit both of these populations. More broadly, realisation of the nexus between prevention of zoonotic diseases and healthy aging from child through to late adulthood is important for the health of humanity in the framework of One Health.

articles.title: Hydrodynamic approximation of particle anisometry in solid lipid nanoparticles: Influence of lipid and emulsifier.
articles.abstract: Solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNPs) may be used as carriers for lipophilic drugs but also offer potential for the formulation of hydrophilic biomacromolecules via surface adsorption. Regarding the latter, specific surface area and particle anisometry are key parameters, yet quantitative methods to assess them for non-spherical particles remain limited. In this study, a hydrodynamic approach based on Perrin's theory for oblate ellipsoids was applied to approximate particle anisometry from dynamic light scattering data. Using this approach, the influence of matrix lipid type, particle size, emulsifier type, and emulsifier concentration on the shape of SLNPs was systematically investigated. Along the triglyceride series trilaurin to tristearin, particle anisometry increased with chain length, consistent with the formation of thinner, more platelet-like particles. Smaller SLNPs exhibited lower anisometry than larger particles. Interfacial effects were pronounced: post-modification with different emulsifiers resulted in marked differences in hydrodynamically approximated anisometry, with sucrose monolaurate-treated systems showing the highest and poloxamer 407-treated systems the lowest apparent anisometry. Increasing the concentration of poloxamer 188 reduced anisometry, whereas increasing the concentration of sucrose monolaurate increased it. Electron microscopic imaging qualitatively confirmed the calculated trends in particle shape. Overall, the presented method provides a practical screening tool for comparing relative changes in SLNP anisometry. It also enables the assessment of formulation-dependent differences in particle shape characteristics, which may be highly relevant for optimizing the adsorption of hydrophilic macromolecules to nanoparticle surfaces.

articles.title: Systematic Multi-Model Toxicological Evaluation and Phytochemical Signatures of Carthamus tinctorius L., Scabiosa comosa, and Their Mixture: Acute and 28-Day Oral Toxicity Studies.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Carthamus tinctorius L. and Scabiosa comosa Fisch. ex Roem. & Schult. are traditional medicinal plants used within the Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and Traditional Mongolian Medicine (TMM) systems in China. Historically, the dried florets of C. tinctorius are administered as an aqueous decoction, typically at 3-10 g/day, and are prescribed to invigorate blood circulation and resolve blood stasis, whereas the capitula of S. comosa are prepared as a decoction or powder, typically at 6-9 g/day, and are utilized to clear heat and detoxify, with traditional indications for liver and pulmonary febrile diseases. However, comprehensive evaluations of their antioxidant properties and toxicological characteristics, particularly regarding their individual and combined applications, remain limited. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to systematically characterize the phytochemical composition, antioxidant capacity, and safety profiles of C. tinctorius, S. comosa, and their combination using multiple extraction strategies and complementary biological models. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Water extracts, ethanol extracts, and sequential water-ethanol extracts were prepared and analyzed by LC-MS/MS and total flavonoid content determination. Their antioxidant capacities were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. The toxicological profiles were investigated using BRL-3A rat hepatocytes, zebrafish embryo toxicity assays, acute oral toxicity studies in mice, and a 28-day repeated-dose oral toxicity study in Wistar rats. RESULTS: LC-MS/MS profiling revealed diverse chemical constituents, including phenolic acids, flavonoids, coumarins, and iridoids. Notably, C. tinctorius exhibited the highest total flavonoid content (TFC), and sequential extraction significantly increased TFC compared to single-solvent extractions. In the antioxidant evaluations, S. comosa demonstrated the most potent antioxidant capacity with the lowest EC50 values. Toxicity varied by concentration and extract type, with water extracts displaying the lowest toxicity. While high concentrations induced developmental abnormalities (e.g., mortality, oedema) in zebrafish, rodent models demonstrated high safety. Acute (5000 mg/kg) and 28-day repeated administrations caused no mortality or severe histopathological lesions, yielding only minor body weight and biochemical fluctuations. CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides a systematic chemical and toxicological evaluation of C. tinctorius, S. comosa, and their combination. These extracts exhibited antioxidant potential and favorable safety profiles in multiple experimental models, providing important evidence for their further development as medicinal or functional food-related products.

articles.title: Ziziphora clinopodioides Flavonoids exerts neuroprotective effects through PI3K/Akt pathway to improve ischemic stroke.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Ziziphora clinopodioides Lam. is a traditional Uyghur medicinal herb used for centuries in Xinjiang, China, to treat cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disorders. According to local ethnopharmacological records, it is traditionally employed to promote blood circulation, remove blood stasis, calm the heart, and relieve chest tightness and palpitations. Modern studies have shown that its total flavonoids (ZCF) possess anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. Ischemic stroke (IS) is a leading cause of death and disability, involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. However, the neuroprotective mechanism of ZCF against IS and its active constituents remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to elucidate the neuroprotective mechanism of ZCF against IS and to identify its potential active flavonoids. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Network pharmacology and transcriptomics were used to predict core pathways, followed by in vitro and in vivo experiments. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, BBB integrity, and PI3K/Akt-related inflammatory/oxidative markers were assessed. The PI3K inhibitor LY294002 was used, and active flavonoids were screened by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and ELISA. RESULTS: Integrated transcriptomics and network pharmacology identified that ZCF modulates the PI3K/Akt pathway. In MCAO/R-treated rats, ZCF reduced cerebral infarction, and preserved neuronal morphology. ZCF protected BBB integrity by restoring ZO-1, Occludin, Claudin-5, reducing MMP-9 and MMP-2 levels, rebalancing the Ang-1/Ang-2 ratio, decreasing NaF permeability, and increasing TEER. ZCF activated PI3K/Akt signaling in both bEnd.3 cells and MCAO/R-treated rat brain tissues, and the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reversed ZCF-mediated regulation of tight junction proteins, matrix metalloproteinases, and Ang-1/Ang-2, suggesting that ZCF preserves BBB integrity at least partly through a PI3K/Akt-dependent mechanism. ZCF inhibited the TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 axis, reduced IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α and MDA, and up-regulated Nrf2 and SOD, and these effects were reversed by LY294002. Molecular docking and MD simulations suggested that Diosmin, Glycitin, and Tilianin may form stable binding with PI3K. Diosmin, Glycitin and Tilianin could significantly restore the activity of PI3K in PC12 cells treated with OGD/R, reduce the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α and MDA, and enhance the activity of SOD. CONCLUSION: Under preconditioning conditions, ZCF maintains BBB and inhibits neuroinflammation and oxidative stress through integrity and PI3K/Akt dependence, thereby exerting anti-IS protection. Diosmin, Glycitin, and Tilianin are potential active flavonoids that may contribute to PI3K/Akt activation.

articles.title: Total Ginsenosides from Panax ginseng Improve Exercise Tolerance in Rats with Spleen Qi Deficiency-like Features: Integrated Metabolomics of Serum and Hepatic Mitochondria-enriched Fractions.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Panax ginseng C.A.Mey. has traditionally been used to replenish Qi and strengthen the spleen, including for poor appetite and weakness associated with spleen deficiency. Ginsenosides are major constituents, but their metabolic effects under spleen Qi deficiency-like conditions remain to be clarified. AIM OF THE STUDY: To evaluate whether total ginsenosides (TGS) improve spleen Qi deficiency-like features in rats and characterize systemic and hepatic metabolic changes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A rat model was established using 50% food restriction combined with repeated weight-loaded swimming, and TGS (75, 150, or 300 mg·kg-1) was administered for 21 days. Body weight, grip strength, swimming endurance, biochemical indices, and mitochondrial ultrastructure were evaluated. Untargeted metabolomic analyses of serum and hepatic mitochondria-enriched fractions were performed in the control (CON), model (MOD), and high-dose TGS (TGS-H) groups, and hepatic SIRT1 and PGC-1α protein expression was measured. Lipid accumulation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and SIRT1 and PGC-1α expression were also examined in oleic acid-treated HepG2 cells. RESULTS: TGS, particularly at 300 mg·kg-1, attenuated the suppression of body-weight gain and improved grip strength and swimming endurance. These functional improvements were accompanied by increased ATP content and ATPase activities and attenuation of mitochondrial ultrastructural abnormalities. After TGS-H treatment, serum levels of several amino acids increased, and lipid profiles shifted toward the control pattern. In hepatic mitochondria-enriched fractions, accumulation of selected fatty acids decreased, and levels of selected organic acids increased. TGS increased hepatic PGC-1α protein expression at all three doses, whereas SIRT1 expression increased significantly only at the high dose. In oleic acid-treated HepG2 cells, increased expression of both proteins was accompanied by reduced lipid accumulation and partial recovery of mitochondrial membrane potential. CONCLUSIONS: In rats with spleen Qi deficiency-like features induced by limited nutritional supply and repeated physical exertion, TGS attenuated the suppression of body-weight gain and improved exercise tolerance, accompanied by changes in energy-related indices. These findings provide experimental support for the traditional use of ginseng to replenish Qi and strengthen the spleen in relation to symptoms of weakness.

articles.title: Zuogui Wan preserves Leydig cell steroidogenesis via G6PD/NADPH/GSH-dependent ferroptosis inhibition in D-galactose-induced hypogonadism.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Zuogui Wan (ZGW), a classical formula for aging-related disorders, may delay reproductive decline, but its effects on late-onset hypogonadism (LOH) remain unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: To investigate the effects and underlying mechanisms of ZGW in LOH using rat and cellular models by integrating serum pharmacochemistry, network pharmacology, and transcriptomic analyses. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A D-galactose-induced accelerated aging rat model was established to evaluate the ameliorative effects of ZGW. Blood-absorbed constituents were identified by UHPLC-MS/MS, and candidate pathways and targets were screened by integrating network pharmacology, testicular transcriptomics, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Mechanistic validation was performed in rat testicular tissues and TM3 Leydig cells, and the functional role of G6PD was further evaluated using G6PDi-1-mediated pharmacological inhibition and G6pdx knockdown/overexpression rescue experiments. RESULTS: ZGW ameliorated D-galactose-induced reproductive endocrine dysfunction and testicular aging-related injury in rats and attenuated injury in TM3 Leydig cells. Based on the identification of 36 blood-absorbed constituents, integrated analyses prioritized G6PD and suggested that it may be involved in redox regulation and ferroptosis-related mechanisms. In vivo and in vitro experiments showed that ZGW restored G6PD-related NADPH/GSH redox homeostasis, strengthened GPX4-dependent defense against lipid peroxidation, attenuated ferroptosis-related injury, and preserved mitochondrial function and StAR/CYP11A1-associated steroidogenesis. Both G6PDi-1 and G6pdx knockdown partially attenuated the effects of ZGW, whereas G6pdx rescue partially restored these changes. CONCLUSIONS: ZGW may alleviate D-gal-induced LOH-like dysfunction by restoring G6PD-related NADPH/GSH homeostasis and GPX4-dependent lipid-peroxide defense. These effects may limit ferroptosis-related injury and preserve the mitochondrial conditions required for StAR/CYP11A1-associated steroidogenesis.

articles.title: Traditional Licorice-Milk Processing of Alangium chinense (Lour.) Harms Reduces Hepatotoxicity and Enhances Bioactivity via EGFR/PI3K/AKT Pathway Modulation.
